questiontext.text: In an adjacency multilist for an undirected graph, what does a single list node represent?

answer.text: One edge, shared and linked into both of its endpoints' lists

feedback.text: Correct — a multilist is edge-oriented; each edge is a single shared node.

answer.text: One vertex and its degree

feedback.text: The multilist is organised around edges, not per-vertex counters.

answer.text: An entire V-length matrix row

feedback.text: That is the adjacency matrix, not a multilist node.

answer.text: A separate copy of the edge for each endpoint

feedback.text: A plain adjacency list duplicates edges; the multilist deliberately does not.

generalfeedback.text: An adjacency multilist is edge-oriented: each edge is one shared node threaded into both endpoints' lists.

questiontext.text: Compared with a plain adjacency list, how many times does an adjacency multilist store each undirected edge?

answer.text: Once — as a single node shared by both endpoints

feedback.text: Correct — the edge node is shared, so it is stored exactly once.

answer.text: Twice — once in each endpoint's list

feedback.text: That is the plain adjacency list; the multilist avoids the duplicate.

answer.text: V times — once per vertex

feedback.text: An edge only involves its two endpoints, not every vertex.

answer.text: Never — edges are recomputed on demand

feedback.text: Edges are stored explicitly as nodes.

generalfeedback.text: A multilist stores each undirected edge once as a shared node, unlike a plain adjacency list which stores it twice.

questiontext.text: The adjacency multilist is best described as which kind of representation?

answer.text: An edge-oriented representation for undirected graphs

feedback.text: Correct — nodes correspond to edges, shared between endpoints.

answer.text: A purely vertex-oriented array of counters

feedback.text: The multilist centres on edge nodes, not per-vertex counters.

answer.text: A dense V×V table of bits

feedback.text: That is the adjacency matrix.

answer.text: A representation only usable for directed graphs

feedback.text: The multilist is designed for undirected graphs.

generalfeedback.text: The multilist is an edge-oriented structure for undirected graphs where each edge is a shared node.

questiontext.text: Why is the shared-edge-node design of a multilist convenient?

answer.text: You can mark an edge as visited once and see it from both endpoints

feedback.text: Correct — a single shared node makes edge marking during traversal easy.

answer.text: It makes edge lookup O(1) like a matrix

feedback.text: Edge lookup still requires walking a list; O(1) lookup is the matrix's trait.

answer.text: It removes the need to store vertices at all

feedback.text: Vertices still head their lists of edge nodes.

answer.text: It converts the graph into a directed graph

feedback.text: The multilist represents the same undirected graph.

generalfeedback.text: Because each edge is one shared node, marking or traversing an edge once is visible from both endpoints — handy in edge-based algorithms.

questiontext.text: In an adjacency multilist, each edge node is linked into the lists of both of its endpoints.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the single edge node belongs to both endpoints' lists.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The whole point of the multilist is that both endpoints share the one edge node.

questiontext.text: A plain adjacency list stores an undirected edge twice, whereas an adjacency multilist stores it only once.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — the multilist's shared node avoids the duplicate the adjacency list keeps.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: An adjacency list does duplicate the edge; the multilist stores it once.

questiontext.text: In an adjacency multilist, each shared node corresponds to one ______ of the graph.

answer.text: edge

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: edge*

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the adjacency multilist are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each undirected edge is represented by exactly one shared node

feedback.text: Yes — that is the defining feature.

answer.text: An edge node is threaded into both of its endpoints' lists

feedback.text: Yes — it is reachable from both endpoints.

answer.text: It duplicates every edge, once per endpoint, like a plain adjacency list

feedback.text: No — the multilist shares one node instead of duplicating.

answer.text: It provides O(1) edge-existence tests like an adjacency matrix

feedback.text: No — O(1) edge tests are the matrix's property, not the multilist's.

generalfeedback.text: Multilist: each edge is one shared node linked from both endpoints, stored once (not duplicated), and it does not give O(1) matrix-style lookups.
